overview: This bill writes into law a National Institutes of Health (NIH) research program on Down syndrome, a genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. The program, called the INCLUDE Project, would fund research on how Down syndrome affects health and development across a person's life, expand clinical trials that include people with Down syndrome, and study related conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and autoimmune disorders, which are more common in this group. It would also support research on better diagnosis, treatment and quality of life for people with Down syndrome and their families. NIH would have to coordinate the work across its institutes, avoid duplicating existing research, consult patient advocates, and report to Congress every two years. The Senate passed it on August 6, 2026, and as of August 10, 2026, it was being held at the desk in the House.
for: Supporters say putting the program into law gives Down syndrome research lasting footing and helps people with the condition get included in clinical trials they have often been left out of.
against: Critics say the bill doesn't provide new funding, so it could shift attention within NIH's existing budget, and that Congress writing specific disease programs into law can limit scientists' flexibility to set priorities.
